# interactive compatibility: paste, source, and the ecosystem

*Generated by `make paste-gate` from `internal/compat` — do not edit by hand.*

**Paste gate: 18 of 18 cases pass.** **Source gate: 2 of 2 installed tools pass** (6 of 8 not installed on the machine that generated this).

**Ecosystem matrix: 4 of 4 installed tools pass** (3 of 7 not installed here).

Oracle: bash 5.3.15(1)-release.

"Pasted bash one-liners and sourced bash scripts fail" is the top
abandonment cause on two independent corpora — 22 first-person accounts
across a decade on HN/Lobsters, and 27 of 62 churn accounts on Reddit.
[docs/compat.md](compat.md) scores bash *scripts* through `gish -c`.
This page covers the two paths that scoreboard does not: text pasted at
an interactive prompt, and real init scripts sourced unmodified.

The distinction is not academic. A pasted line goes through bracketed
paste, the line editor, history expansion, the diagnostics pass and the
accept-or-continue decision before the interpreter sees it — five places
a line can change meaning, none of them exercised by running a script.

## Paste gate

Each case is pasted into a real interactive gish on a pty, as a
terminal delivers a paste, and Enter is pressed. Output is read from
between the OSC 133 semantic marks, so there is no guessing where the
prompt ended. bash is the oracle: the same text is run through real
bash and the results must agree.

| case | result | provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| command substitution | ✅ | the single most-pasted construct; named in HN 2024-01-23 |
| backticks | ✅ | older one-liners and README snippets still use them |
| && and \|\| chains | ✅ | every install one-liner |
| one-shot environment prefix | ✅ | `FOO=bar cmd` — the idiom people paste from CI docs |
| while loop on one line | ✅ | r/commandline paste threads; a compound command typed as one line |
| for loop with brace expansion | ✅ | brace expansion is bash-only and is pasted constantly |
| [[ ]] test with pattern match | ✅ | bash conditional expressions in pasted snippets |
| process substitution | ✅ | `diff <(a) <(b)` — named as a fish blocker |
| unquoted URL with a query string | ✅ | `mpv https://…?v=X` — a day-one quit in fish and unconfigured zsh |
| unquoted URL with bracket characters | ✅ | the same class: [ and ] are glob metacharacters too |
| single quotes protect everything | ✅ | install lines that embed $ and ! inside single quotes |
| heredoc pasted as one block | ✅ | config-writing one-liners in READMEs |
| arithmetic and parameter expansion together | ✅ | the mixed-expansion lines that break naive parsers |
| pipeline with quoting | ✅ | grep/awk/sed one-liners, the bread and butter of a paste |
| escaped newline continuation | ✅ | multi-line install commands pasted whole |
| history expansion: !! with a command prefix | ✅ | `sudo !!` — the most-named muscle memory in the corpus |
| history expansion: !$ last argument | ✅ | !$ is second only to !! in the accounts |
| a bang inside single quotes does not expand | ✅ | the classic zsh papercut: 'don't!' at a prompt |

## Source gate

The named breakers, sourced **unmodified** as installed on the machine,
then probed for what they defined. Differential again: the same
load-and-probe script through bash and through gish.

A tool that is not installed is listed as such rather than dropped —
"every case we ran passed" means nothing without the list of what was
not run.

| tool | result | provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| nvm | — not installed here | the single most-named breaker in the churn accounts |
| rbenv init | — not installed here | named in the abandonment accounts alongside nvm |
| pyenv init | — not installed here | same class as rbenv; ships a bash-specific init |
| conda shell hook | — not installed here | conda init's output is a named breaker |
| rvm | — not installed here | the Ruby half of the nvm story |
| virtualenv activate | ✅ | `.venv/bin/activate` — the most-sourced script in Python work |
| virtualenvwrapper | — not installed here | named in the corpus; defines a dozen functions at source time |
| direnv hook | ✅ | `eval "$(direnv hook bash)"` is in a great many rc files |

## Ecosystem matrix

The point of implementing bash's hook surface is that the tools people
already have keep working. This is that claim, measured: each tool is
installed unmodified, **its own documented init line** is sourced, and
its behavior is asserted in a live interactive gish on a pty — the
prompt renders, the widget binds, the environment changes on cd.

| tool | result | what it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| starship | ✅ | the prompt renders through starship's own bash init |
| oh-my-posh | ✅ | the prompt renders through oh-my-posh's own bash init |
| zoxide | — not installed here | `z` jumps — the user's own zoxide, not gish's native jumper |
| atuin | — not installed here | atuin's Ctrl-R binding is installed |
| direnv | ✅ | the .envrc applies on cd, through direnv's own hook |
| mise | — not installed here | mise activates and stays usable |
| fzf | ✅ | fzf's Ctrl-T widget is bound, from --bash or the packaged key-bindings file |

## Honesty notes

- The source gate's coverage depends on what is installed where it runs.
  CI runners carry a different set than a developer laptop, so the
  numbers in this file describe the machine that generated it, and the
  gate enforces "no fewer passes among the tools that *were* present".
- The paste gate asks bash the same question wherever the two paths ask
  the same thing. History expansion is the exception: it is off in
  bash's non-interactive mode, so those cases name the equivalent
  command they pose to bash instead, in the corpus, where it can be
  argued with.
- A pass means the pasted text behaved identically, not that every
  construct in that family is supported.
- Regressions fail CI (`make paste-gate-check`).
